messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 30
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: North American
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: Carpenter
- Trauma Type: Witnessed other trauma
- Pcl5: 61

**Case Vignette: Marcus**

Marcus is a thirty-year-old carpenter who has been married for four years. He works for a small residential construction company, framing houses and doing finish work — a trade he learned from his uncle as a teenager and has always taken pride in. Until about eighteen months ago, he describes himself as someone who was "pretty steady," a man who liked the physical rhythm of the work, came home tired in a good way, and spent weekends with his wife hiking or watching football with friends.

Everything shifted on an ordinary Tuesday afternoon on a job site. Marcus was working on the second floor of a house under construction when a coworker — a man named Derek, someone he had worked alongside for nearly three years — fell through an unsupported section of subfloor. Marcus was close enough to hear the crack of the wood and close enough to see Derek fall. He was the first person to reach him. Derek had landed badly and was conscious but badly injured, his leg fractured in a way Marcus describes only as "wrong — just completely wrong." Marcus held him, tried to keep him calm, and waited for the ambulance. Derek survived, but the image of those twelve minutes on that concrete slab has never left Marcus.

In the weeks that followed, Marcus returned to work because he felt he had no real reason not to. Derek was alive. The accident was investigated, the site was corrected, and everyone moved on — or appeared to. Marcus found he could not. He began waking at three or four in the morning with his heart hammering, certain he had heard something breaking. His wife, Renata, would find him sitting at the kitchen table in the dark, unable to explain what he was doing there. He started having intrusive flashes during the day — the sound of splintering wood, the look on Derek's face — that arrived without warning and left him shaken and distant for hours.

At work, Marcus has become hypervigilant in ways that have begun to affect his performance. He checks and rechecks flooring before he steps anywhere, even on structures he himself has built and knows to be sound. He avoids certain tasks on upper floors when he can, finding reasons to stay on the ground level. His supervisor has noticed and commented, not unkindly, but Marcus feels a deep shame about it that he cannot shake. He was always the reliable one, the one others looked to. Now he feels like a liability.

At home, Renata describes him as "somewhere else." He is irritable in ways that surprise even him — snapping at small things, then feeling guilty and withdrawing. He has stopped watching football with his friends, stopped returning most calls. He tells himself he is tired, that it is the job, but he knows it is more than that. He and Renata have had long conversations about it, and she is patient and worried in equal measure. Intimacy between them has become strained; Marcus feels a persistent numbness that he cannot will away, a flatness that sits over everything even on days when nothing particular has gone wrong.

He does not sleep well. He avoids driving past the street where the job site was, even though it adds fifteen minutes to his commute. He has not been back to see Derek, though Derek has reached out several times. Marcus knows this is not right. He thinks about calling. He does not call.

What troubles Marcus most, sitting in a therapist's office for the first time and turning his wedding ring slowly on his finger, is not any single symptom but a larger fear — that the person he was before that Tuesday afternoon is simply gone, and that the man sitting here now, watchful and exhausted and ashamed, is who he is going to be from now on.
